items.body: Purest Form Resistance Dais Records Despite its brief fifteen minute runtime, there’s a meal to be made out of LA trio Purest Form’s latest EP, their debut on Dais, both in terms of attitude and presentation, as well as what its selection of very clear influences might portend for the larger post-industrial landscape. Drawing upon familiar markers of 90s electronic aggression, Resistance provides a tight test case for their read on that historical moment. Opener “Animal” functions as a strong calling card for Purest Form, showing both their capacity for a catchy, heavily processed guitar riff as well as Story Beeson’s acidic growl that’s part grindcore, part death metal. Factor in just the right amount of backing programming and an easily chantable chorus and it becomes both cathartic and anthemic in short order. It is, to be glib, exactly the type of thrashing industrial rock glory which KMFDM have been failing to recapture for the past couple of decades. Much of the rest of the EP’s made up of densely programmed two-minute wipeouts jammed up with breaks, more heavily processed guitar now functioning more for colour than riffs, and more spleen and vile being vented. If that sounds on paper fairly akin to digital hardcore, listening to “Break” and “More” will do little to dissuade that presumption. “Beyond Terror” acts as a quick riposte to this frenetic pace, offering post-hardcore chug while the vocals cut through equivocations about the killings of Palestinians – “call it what you like, it’s genocide.” And then there’s the closing cover. Fifteen or twenty years back, an industrial metal act doing a straightforward version of The Prodigy’s “Breathe” would have felt awkwardly retrograde. However, a full three decades on from the original release and overdriven into the red to the point that it’s difficult to distinguish original tracks from sampled ones, Purest Form’s take on “Breathe” feels like the best sort of “oh shit, they’re covering this?” moment at the end of a packed and sweaty basement show. In discussing the appeal of the 90s sources Pures Form borrow from it’s important to not overstate how new they might be to the band; both Beeson and guitarist/programmer Madi Woodward both have lengthy rap sheets with slews of hardcore and metal acts going back a decade or so. But there’s no question that a combination of their backgrounds beyond industrial and the historical space separating Resistance from those acts helps invigorate their dense and furious angle on them. Buy it. RESISTANCE by PUREST FORM The post Purest Form, “Resistance” appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: A saxophonist by nature, Calum Builder couldn’t help but think of the brass instrument while salvaging old church organ pipes in Northern Denmark, regarding the organ as “another aerophone working with a different kind of breath.” Honoring the prophecy of his surname, he built a reconstructed organ portable enough to take on tour. Enlisting the aid of vocalists Johanna Sulkunen and Zola Mennenöh, he combines these sounds with fragment of psalms, creating a sound that is part palimpsest, part excavation. The opening tracks are each a quarter-hour in length, allowing the listener to dive deep into the waters of divinity. “Where Can I Go” takes its lead from Psalm 139 and pairs beautifully with Andrzej Pietrewicz & Haiyue Zhu’s #10 from last year. At first there are only forlorn taps and tones, a hint of flute, a sense of desolation: hot winds blowing across even hotter sand. The darker tones come across as howls: the keening cry of the djinn. After five minutes, the harmonies emerge like an oasis, beginning the thought (“Where can I go?”) without revealing the full passage. As the vocalists sing louder and shift intonation, their repetitions become prayers. The reconstructed organ recedes, clearing space for their words to waft to the heavens. A vocal loop rides atop an organ drone, then breaks free, growing faster and more insistent. Listeners unfamiliar with the psalm may miss the underlying comfort in the unspoken words that follow, communicated only through the breath of the pipes until the closing, consoling minute. The opening timbre of “Surely” is like that of a train horn, recalling the steam engines of earlier times. One begins to muse on the similarities between instruments. Apart from being a punchline in the movie “Airplane!”, the word surely is found dozens of times in Scripture and most famously in the 23rd Psalm. Builder chooses the lesser known Psalm 139:11-12, NIV: If I say, “Surely the darkness will hide me and the light become night around me,” even the darkness will not be dark to you; the night will shine like the day, for darkness is as light to you. Behind the gorgeous vocals, a drone of darkness rises like a shroud, eclipsing but not eliminating the words. Again – as in the psalm – the overlying tone is foreboding, like an accumulated mass of daily troubles, but the underlying message is that God is still present, just as the notes remain in the pipes even after they have been removed from the church organ. The thin tendrils of sound that close the piece are like the last vestiges of night retreating from the day as the piece topples. without pause into “Is As Light.” This final movement contains some of the highest vocal notes and lowest organ notes, a contrast that underlines the theme. The album title quotes the Latin Eadem mutata resurgo, which relates not only to the logarithmic spiral, but to the nature of the soul. As famous Swiss mathematician Jakob Bernoulli writes, “The logarithmic spiral may be used as a symbol either of fortitude and consistency in adversity, or of the human body, which after all these changes, even after death, will be restored to its exact and perfect self.” Calum Builder’s album may refer more to the first, but ultimately points the way to the second. (Richard Allen)

Magic Hour is both accessible and deeply experimental with its mutant ambient approach. The sonic palette employs clicks and clacks, echoes, mechanical whirs, lost terrestrial train whistles, melodic forms, shattering forms, and human murmurs, sometimes slowing or speeding up local fields to gain an emotional edge. Sharp, jarring cuts where one familiar sound instantly morphs into a new field. Drawing on all available sonic materials—including instrumental sounds, electronics, fragments of recorded audio, and environmental sounds—FeLid creates tracks and improvisational live performances through continuous processes of deconstruction and reconstruction. So many examples. Sounds with backwards envelopes, where the natural decay of a noise happens before its sharp impact. Freezing a specific moment or target in complete temporal suspension. Magic Hour is the second album by Tokyo-based artist FeLid, who combines improvisational and accidental guitar sounds, lyrical ambient drones, and high-definition sound editing. His practice is designed as a shared exploration of the relationship between sound and space, inviting audiences to experience and discover these connections together in real time. FeLid is the solo project of Kazutoshi Eguchi. He is known as a member of the post-hardcore band the north end and as a co-organizer of the festival platform MIMINOIMI. A collage of percussion instruments :: I am imagining dry mountain water, such as found in a Japanese rock garden. “Karesansui in the air #2” (5:14) opens into a collage of percussion instruments, wooden objects being tapped or struck, a curiously nourishing soup of casual fast easy flowing sounds. Here the passage of time is an objective measure. “Hello, World” (3:37) might be a welcome transparent soup of small items. Behind everything there is steamy condensation dripping and falling into a puddle on the ground, forming clusters with little gaps. Next the beat is bubbling and walking by itself, the feeling brings little scenes that open and close, and return, “Magic hour (disco)” (4:37). The ticking of the clock machinery is dark and hidden things are happening all around. The next thing I remember, I awakened in an “Environmental Mood” (3:13). We are washing stuff in the cave, bumping and scrubbing, spilling water and tossing things around, the scrubbing is the beat. Time to go to work. “Rotate Dub” (3:30) has musical lathes, a running motor sound of some kind, chattering and rattles, perhaps close views of many different motors not all at once, the power tools sing and purr. Do you feel like an afternoon rain shower? “Yuudachi Dub #2” (2:44) brings a different lathe creature here, chattering away faster, sometimes speeding like a demon, with a jittery beat, moving really quickly along, faces appear flattened in the direction they are traveling, the clock on board stretches. Our spaceship appears to move very slowly. “”Rotate Dub” (3:30) has musical lathes, a running motor sound of some kind, chattering and rattles, perhaps close views of many different motors not all at once, the power tools sing and purr. Do you feel like an afternoon rain shower?” ~Robin B. James Hold on, this next track is less than a minute in duration, “Akirame Mo Kanzin” (0:58). Metal stuff and small percussion instruments are being tapped, played backwards and forwards, very busy until the end, that occurs in an apparently irreversible succession from the past, through the present, and into the future. Now I am floating in the dark waters, “Harmonics Dub” (1:51), barely bobbing on the surface. I love the sound of guitar harmonics, textures made by energizing the strings, a mandolin being dusted off, searching for something. This turns out to lead into a haunted house, where we can play ping pong, “Sense of Gradation” (5:56) blends drone like textures with the steady ping pong tok tok tok sounds, a sound collage of real-world noises that have been warped, looped, and recontextualized into an abstract sonic experience, never busy, accenting the constant drone​ of imaginary wire strings being provoked, while the ping pong activities continue, proving the ability to use magic related to time. FeLid is also a member of MIMINOIMI, an organizing collective dedicated to exploring ambient and experimental music from multiple perspectives, and is involved in the planning and production of the urban festival Ambient / Week. Magic Hour is available on ato.archives. [Bandcamp] Magic Hour by FeLidThe post FeLid :: Magic Hour (ato.archives) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

They wouldrelease three albums in the 1970s and be yet another inhabitant of that deep RPI back bench. Farbeyond the many well-known classic Italian pop/rock bands getting respect and attention on thesurface, there were so many other bands who never made the front bench. Even many prog fans whoembrace the existence of RPI may not have heard of a band like Salis. And yet, so many of theseobscure groups have work that is worthy of attention even if it is not the full-blown progressiverock that would follow later in the decade.While most people will point to their "proggiest" third album, it is the this debut that is of mostinterest to me. It joins a crucial group of Italian proto-RPI bands who set the stage for what wascoming just around the bend. This group of bands ranges from Italian pop to blues rock to psychrock, all pushing the barriers of their own zone while releasing work that was not quite fullyformed progressive rock. Some are just okay and some are quite exciting. This is one of the betterones in my view. While you have the short song format and bluesy-jazzy psych rock variations, theirsecret weapon is their passion and an amazing feel for memorable little motifs that are not alwayspredictable. They begin to seep into your head after just a couple spins, and I think it may besttheir other two releases that get most of the attention. This first Salis album is a must for RPIfans who like stuff like Fabio Celi, Il Mucchio, and Equipe 84. Sometimes the special sauce is justyouth.

It was 1994, the era of indie and alternative rock; much had changed since 1992, the year of his previous studio album. That shift may well have influenced the group of musicians he assembled, a lineup that was anything but accidental, featuring Arto Lindsay on guitar (previously with the Lounge Lizards, John Zorn, and Marc Ribot), John Medeski on organ, Bill Ware on vibraphone (formerly of The Jazz Passengers and Groove Collective), and Bebel Gilberto, the daughter of Jo�o Gilberto."A Long Time Ago" begins to unfurl a descending, subtle mist amidst soft layers of guitar, synthesizers, and percussion, while the vocals, initially a mere whisper with a dreamlike, psychedelic quality, gradually begin to reveal their full power. Then, a sonic explosion, driven by distorted guitars and a prominent bassline, sweeps through everything in "Angels." Lyrics full of defiance and poetry, philosophical, too, delivered with deep emotion and vocal power; that vocal timbre also always held a touch of Adrian Belew, at least in its more melodic sense. And when he hit those high notes, leaving just the strumming guitar, accompanied by the bass and his voice declaring he was ready, it was a magnificent moment. It opened up from within like an explosion of light, unlike anything seen before in his career, quite the paradox for his darkest album."Crash" bursts in with a syncopated rhythm, like shattering glass; it is one of those albums where each track is sonically conceived in relation to the one preceding it, adding extra value. A dissonant guitar, paired with unconventional drumming, lends a unique touch, evoking a walk through ruins. It is as if the Smashing Pumpkins and Soundgarden were attempting a funk sound; that is how unusual the blend is, yet it succeeds brilliantly, driven by that deliberately fractured rhythm... all held together by the glue of the vocals."A Self-Made Man" has a hypnotic rhythm and a melody that gradually reveals itself to be magical and spellbinding, as he sings: "Well, I'll trade you my potential, mental illness for your bad teeth. And now we have a black market. A black market for designer genes. They've taken everything from you: the way you walk, the way you smile, the sound of your voice. I don't even know who you are. Who are you now? I am a self-made man (I have nothing left to give) I am a self-made man (I have nothing left to lose)"That is how groundbreaking this album was, and not just musically; although I like several of his solo albums, this one holds a very special place."Back In The Box" sounds modern; the guitars, featuring Arto Lindsay on the more experimental side and David Byrne on the funk side, combined with the bass and the melody in David's phrasing, create a sort of deconstructed Krautrock, albeit heavily distorted, as is the case across most of the album. The familiar Latin rhythms take on a mysterious air here, as evidenced by "Sad Song", while the energy never flags; John Medeski contributes a "gritted-teeth" rhythmic intensity that maintains its drive regardless of genre shifts."Nothing At All" reveals more of Byrne's true essence: he lays his voice bare, stretching notes to their limit amidst dissonant guitar rhythms and a sense of mystery that offers no clues as to his intentions. Only at the very end does he begin to unravel the harmonic thread, a move clearly planned from the start, concluding with instrumental codas driven by heavy cymbal work alongside distorted guitar and organ."My Love Is You" opens with bossa nova-style acoustic guitar notes, then shifts into a stark contrast to what came before, courtesy of Bill Ware. "Lilies Of The Valley" returns to playful, experimental rhythms, driven by a powerful bass and drum foundation, packed with Groove, that builds in intensity while the funk guitar seems to lock in perfectly with David. The finale is a marvelous duet between Todd Turkisher's drums and Bill Ware's vibraphone."You & Eye" keeps the syncopated funk going, with David playing the clavinet, and features a very delicate chorus that contrasts with the melody's frenetic rhythm. He hadn't lost that knack for composing songs that strike a direct chord, quite the opposite; here, there are echoes of African music in the style of Salif Keita. With Dolette McDonald on backing vocals, the same one who had worked with Sting, Stevie Winwood, and many others."Strange Ritual" is one of the key tracks, where that opening mist returns, dark and dangerous, like Naked City, while the lyrics go: "A man sits in a field, contemplating his crops. Scenes that disgust me, I see myself, I felt awe, I felt disgust, I felt bliss, I felt lust, It is not unusual, I saw people in a remote village, proudly sporting their digital watches. I saw a young Indonesian woman, possessed by the spirit of the Ninja Turtles. I saw palatial mansions with decaying decor and human furniture. I saw a legislature of women being courted by corporate lobbyists. A town whose own inhabitants do not even remember its name. We have a strange ritual. We keep it to ourselves. We are lost in love"There is a restrained violence, and gradually, in the vein of King Crimson's "Indiscipline", a section marked by calm and camouflaged rage, by a lurking violence, erupts; the vocals shift in tandem with the intensity of the music and the musicality of the words. From the mist emerges a nightmare where playing the lead role isn't frightening, because we are in control. We will never hear a more rock-oriented, fully committed David Byrne; it brings to mind King Crimson's improvisations on Starless and Bible Black. It is almost on that level."Buck Naked" is essentially just the guitar, John Medeski's organ, and David's vocals, with him giving it his all, whether in moments of presence or absence. It plays with the contrasts between calm and rage seen in his Psycho Killer era. Yet there is no nostalgia here; he breaks away from the past to launch a new phase, unafraid to keep experimenting and embracing new influences, much as he would later do with the Balanescu Quartet on 1997's Feelings. However, nowhere else is there such a sincere, honest, and unadorned outpouring of the heart as on this album, which, like the other side of a mirror, features his surname spelled in reverse.

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Once again fabulously illustrated by Annette Appleton in a captivating pictorial style?part na�ve, part naturalistic, and slightly dreamlike?*Estanyo Nord* is the last album by the English duo The Light Afternoon, aka Steve Newland, the ultra-perfectionist multi-instrumentalist, and Annette Appleton, the singer-illustrator with a shy, fairy-like voice. To illustrate the cover of *Estanyo Nord* and the inside poster, Annette was determined to depict the Panorama house and its surroundings as a veritable Garden of Eden, with a profusion of very real animals?mostly birds and cats, but also dogs and a gecko?in a visionary and imaginative style that makes this miraculous bestiary seem surreal and symbolic.The album tells the story of this exotic miniature Walden, a little lost paradise, just a stone's throw from the road and a short walk from the sea, and of its inhabitants? whether human (Ana Cirema and all the other souls of the household) or non-human?mostly cats ("Our Time In The Tin North")?who thrived in Panorama under a dark velvet sky streaked with shooting stars. Conceptually and structurally, *Estanyo Nord* is divided into two distinct parts ("Part One: Anacirema," "Part Two: Estanyo Nord"), like the two sides of a vinyl record, each consisting of four tracks, 4 or 5 minutes per track, for a total running time of 38 minutes?thus respecting the spirit and constraints of vinyl records from their heyday. All of this is significant because *Estanyo Nord* draws heavily on the past?from nostalgic memories of Steve and Annette's personal histories to the musical past of everyone who lived through the '80s to the fullest, in a way that was deceptively carefree yet truly full of hope, filled with both certainties and doubts. " "I don't know what makes me happy, I just know what makes me sad, I do my best to remember all the things that make me glad" ("All Of These Things," luminous memories of Malta, France, and Spain) "Musically, Estanyo Nord is very different from our previous album because Steve didn't want to make *The History of Mr. Puffin Man?The Sequel*" (dixit Annette). One couldn't put it better. As dynamic and assertive as the previous album was languid, gentle, and undulating, *Estanyo Nord* has categorically moved away from the dark symphonic prog of La Renaissance or Dead Can Dance, with the instrumental sounds and rhythmic programming here very clearly oriented toward synth-pop. But both albums share the same melancholy and a highly cinematic approach to music, with subtle touches of modulation and tense minor chords. This is particularly evident from the very start of "Wide Open Highway Road Movie," with its *Midnight Express*-like atmosphere, its sharp guitar chords and solos set against highway rhythms, and its synths so distinctly '80s that you can almost hear that faint vintage hiss that followed each synth note, following the strange hum of the electric current that had set them vibrating. With a slower sequenced tempo, "The Girl from Panorama" is more reminiscent of Kraftwerk or the early Human League. Meanwhile, the more high-energy "Anacirema" and "Estanyo Nord"?true hit potential?blend new wave rock and dance music much as New Order did a few years ago. Those who enjoyed the symphonic harmonies of *The History Of Mr Puffin Man* might prefer "The Paradero" and "All of These Things," with their delicate, haunting melodies, piano arpeggios, mysterious or commanding synths, subtle vocal arrangements, and that guitar that reminds me of Pulsar's *Gorlitz* (1989) in a slightly decadent, fin-de-si�cle (20th-century) atmosphere that evokes Bowie's legendary and unconventional *Low*. This European atmosphere is present with even more tenderness and romanticism on the slow "Watching the Perseids," a small, classically influenced pocket symphony. "Our Time in the Tin North" is closer to the atmospheric post-prog of Soup or North Atlantic Oscillation or the dreamy electronica of Tangerine Dream's latest albums, which should appeal to most of us. But regardless of our musical preferences and how open-minded we are in this regard, it would be a shame to miss this precious opportunity to own such an artistic work?one that is as valuable for its visual presentation as for its musical content. At first glance, it may seem relatively far removed from the usual canons of progressive rock, but ultimately, it is as universal as beauty itself.

That is a good thing, all too often find something immediately likeable, then wonder why I liked it a week later I hate it. But the technicality of all the players involved pushes it well beyond a garage rock band in any conventional sense. I love that they are a not a paint by numbers neo rock band. This is a band pushing musical boundaries, and I love the direction that they are taking. I love their earlier album 'Heart of a Cherry Pit Sun', but this album enters a whole new realm. This is an album well worth checking out, if your penchant is for progressive Jazz, Classical, black metal... etc. etc....In fact, if you really love the progression of progressive rock music, then this is not a band to be missed.

items.body: Review by alainPP — Uncompromising art rock for a fresh sound, minimalist and captivating alternative electro-prog."My Blistering Mind" boasts a distinctive sound, phrased vocals, and electronic, synth-heavy orchestration reminiscent of Porcupine Tree. A final mantra-like repetition of the gentle chorus shifts between pop, cold wave, and Bowie-esque dance-pop-rock, all set to poignant lyrics about mental fragility. "The Mandatory Prize" features a synthetic riff on electric piano, a long, melancholic, and pervasive melody set to lyrics by Dick, with a sound reminiscent of Steve Wilson. Malcolm's voice is ever-present, pale, cold, and robotic, mirroring the synth pads in a new prog style. But that riff is truly gut-wrenching. "Never Really Felt Like Home," with its ambient, hypnotic, and contemplative intro, and Kathryn's deep flute, is a symbol of tranquility. The piccolo allows for a drift into a cinematic-melancholic space where the low guitar solo amplifies this beatific, solemn instrumental. "Smile, Smile, Smile," already seen on the EP, has a haunting metronomic sound on the vibrating bass, the keyboard unfolding, flirting with Esth�sie, the addictive vocals leading to saturation. An electronic Wilson, like his side project No-Man. A stressful, redundant finale leading to musical madness through its endless repetition, the lyrics cruelly explaining this moment of schizoid disarray. "Intermission," as its name suggests, is an instrumental on bass and drums with a jazzy piano, a way of dreaming about the evolution of jazz today. The ensuing Mellotron chills the ears before the colorful piano nods to the works of Joe Jackson."Parallel Lives," with its hushed vocals and contemplative ballad-like feel, sees Kathryn's guitar work on the chorus amplify its solemnity. The effective rhythmic foundation drives this lament, reminiscent of Springsteen's "Streets of Philadelphia." The eponymous track plunges into the depths of Wavy's pop. "Eversion," one of the longer pieces, meanders with lyrics reminiscent of Kate Bush, its orchestration blending neoclassical, synth, and electronic elements, inspired by Steve Wilson. A piano and synth interlude precedes the electric return and Malcolm's vocals, sly, dark, and haughty. The guitar solo brightens the ear, and the sound returns with hypnotic, syncopated percussion, amplifying the progressive, schizophrenic feel. "Pretty Blue Fox" opens with a modern, electro-synth feel, reminiscent of Tangerine Dream in the 70s. It's a blend of electro and prog, with a satisfying mid-section, scraping away at the repetitive sounds of Philip Glass for a restrained, immersive, orgasmic finale ? pure bliss. "Just Another Thing" returns to new prog rock with its piercing, guttural vocals; you'll want to try these breathless vocalizations yourself. There's a hint of Bowie, a sound reminiscent of Simple Minds, a dynamic track with a neo-Marillion-esque keyboard solo, recounting Malcolm's retinal mishaps. "Dropping The Mask" is another instrumental with an electrified, upbeat tempo and bouncy keyboard, a nod to Tangerine Dream in the 80s ? groovy, energetic, and catchy. "Just Hold On (Pts 1 & 2)" opens with a religious, elegiac intro, the soaring choir drifting into hyperspace?a fitting way to escape this groundbreaking album. A striking mix of languid atmosphere and archaic feel, thanks to a guitar emerging from a cloud of Olympus, the solo spreading to the heavens. Malcolm finally appears on this melting synth, the drums merely controlling the rhythm. A solemn ambiance is created by the double bass, the deep vocals, the ephemeral piano, and the final, melancholic guitar outro, a meditative and hopeful finale. A truly beautiful and contemplative ending. "My Blistering Mind," in a shorter, perhaps faster version, and "The Mandatory Prize" are released as radio edits, destined for the airwaves of a better world.HATS OFF GENTLEMEN IT'S ADEQUATE blends vocal and purely instrumental tracks, delivering electronic art-rock with contemporary classical touches. A modern progressive rock sound for the new millennium. (4.5)

items.body: Review by alainPP — NORTH SEA ECHOES, nothing new except for extending their first offering: heavier, more melancholic, more pervasive."A Time of Innocence and Purpose," with its bass and hypnotic, unsettling electro sample, is featured on LUNATIC SOUL. A beautiful ascent with Ray taking the lead, where things become much more interesting. A kind of GILDENLOW and pugnacious OSI hybrid, thanks to that captivating voice that makes all the difference. The ambient, intimate atmosphere makes you close your eyes and dream along to the edgy riff. "Enjoy The View" delves deeper into the electro-synthetic sound with its two-tone vocals and addictive instrumentation. The industrial riff, a sound effect on the thunderous breakdown, the keyboard undulating in a new dark-wave style. The magic works and endures with the energy of the invigorating chorus over the haunting verse, the haunting, dark outro. "Good Enough" features a crystalline, airy, stereo acoustic arpeggio reminiscent of the good old days. The raw, spoken-word vocals are laid over it, creating a country evening feel. The warm crescendo, with Ray as the sonic hero, evokes a dark Louisiana vibe with animals singing in the background: sublime and utterly simple, surfing on the atmospheric. "I'll Leave A Light On" kicks off with a fat riff, a melancholic nod to Katatonia. The pre-screamed vocals over the powerful sound, the chorus like something out of the mainstream era: the nostalgia is amplified by a punchy guitar solo bursting with notes. An added choir graces this track, which flows effortlessly, nothing new but well executed, finally on Fates Warning. "All Fall Away" boasts a bouncy bass beat. A dark, monolithic feel, redolent of Eurythmics in a heavy version, for this primal alternative drift. The guitar twists and turns, illuminating the space, the beat becomes oppressive, reminiscent of PARADISE LOST with Ray's voice, the chorus, then the beat abruptly stopping."Revenge," with its Wavy-esque guitar, surfs on the scales of THE CURE. This decadent rock descends to the realm of electro-pop, a softer DEPECHE MODE, Ray bribing his vocal cords. A repetitive, melancholic finale, far removed from prog rock. "Villains Or Saints" returns to mainstream, mainstream rock with its heavy melody, surfing once again on FATES WARNING. The haunting, synthetic rhythm builds and creates a heavy guitar space over the velvety keyboard. Ray conducts this masterful string piece, always effortless yet captivating, this timeless ballad. "What Is And What Was What," with its dark, ambient, mysterious intro and that wind that seems to come from nowhere. Vocals over a guitar arpeggio, choir over organ, hairs shiver. The bass resonates, clears the speakers, the pleasure of having this vibrant, body-piercing sound, like an arrow piercing your heart. "All That Comes After" returns to edgy rock, energized by its catchy melody. A B-side track that doesn't offer anything new, however, except perhaps to test the stereo image on the atmospheric drift. This melodic sound takes you back to the previous millennium. "How To Cast A Shadow" concludes, the new-wave vibe with its heady keyboard, as fat as the 'metroganic' drums, Ray weaving through this dark, hybrid, alternative slow jam. The mantra-like latency for dancing, swaying with his wife, the guitar both melancholic and slide-like. The feeling of navigating a bayou. A heavy guitar solo, the sound that makes you headbang, the refrain of 80s hard rock bands, I'm sucked into this musical spiral. The finale features Ray clinging to the primal synth, shh... Silence remains a constant presence throughout the album, with its enveloping notes.NORTH SEA ECHOES pushes their identity further with a heavy, dark approach, evolving with the addition of electronic elements to delve into the ghosts of the past, temptation, and reflection. (3.75)

items.body: The chorus of “Don’t Try” turns an old piece of street wisdom into a hook: “Don’t try piss on me and tell me it’s raining”. The man it is aimed at takes the credit for work he did not do, hands out promises that come to nothing, expects the overtime as standard and treats one late morning as an offence. Past him stand all the others: the smile that turns into a betrayal, the boasting about how easily things arrive, the liberties taken without a second thought. The last verse hands the accusation back, on the old line about the three fingers that point home whenever one goes out. Messenjah open Social Commentary with it, seven tracks of reggae made with The Aarons Brothers and released on Reload Records in April 2025. They have played roots reggae since forming in Kitchener, Ontario in 1981, and became the first Canadian reggae band signed to a major label when Warner Music Canada took Rock You High and put the music on national radio here for the first time. That was the second door Rupert “Ojiji” Harvey had opened, after Crack of Dawn, the Toronto soul group he co-founded, became the first Black Canadian band to sign a major deal. He has led Messenjah since the mid-1980s, through Reggae Sunsplash in Montego Bay, a Juno for Catch De Vibe, and a night in 1998 playing for Nelson Mandela at Toronto’s SkyDome. items.body: Zadisphere, an independent dark ritual techno project, published the video “Cathedral” on its official YouTube channel on September 9, 2026. Zadisphere makes a sound that mixes dark ritual techno with cinematic electronics and hypnotic rhythms, combining gothic and baroque elements, pipe organs, strings and choirs with analog sequences. “Cathedral” is a standalone video release; no tied single, EP or label has been confirmed. Zadisphere’s ‘Cathedral’ follows a steady run of new tracks “Cathedral” arrived in a run of near-weekly uploads from the project through August and September 2026, including “Czas / Time” on August 12, “Monolith Threshold” on September 1, “Ritual” on September 3, a remix of Ludwik Sempoliński’s “Ten wąsik” on September 11, “Nienazwane / Unnamed” on September 14 and “Po drugiej stronie / The other side” on September 16. No tracklist, formats or streaming availability have been confirmed for “Cathedral” beyond the YouTube upload. About Zadisphere Behind Zadisphere is a solo artist who treats mood and atmosphere as the project’s real subject, with sound built to serve that focus rather than the other way around. Its stated direction combines dark ritual techno, cinematic electronics and hypnotic rhythms with gothic and baroque influences, using pipe organs, strings, choirs and analog sequences. The project’s YouTube channel was created in January 2024, but its run of released tracks and videos began in August 2026 with “Czas / Time”, followed within weeks by “Monolith Threshold”, “Ritual” and “Cathedral”. Zadisphere has no confirmed label, Discogs entry or Wikipedia page. The project is also present on Instagram and maintains an official website. “Cathedral” is its latest video release.

items.body: Old Europa Cafe releases four new albums and three reissues on 23 October 2026, all as limited digipak CDs. The Italian power electronics, noise and dark ambient label, founded in Pordenone in 1983 by Rodolfo Protti, groups the batch around three reissues from the catalogue of Atrax Morgue, two new records tied to Swedish musician Nordvargr, and new albums from Black Leather Jesus and The Rita’s back catalogue. Atrax Morgue’s ‘Alive and Dead’, ‘Paranoia’ and ‘Pathophysiology’ reissued Atrax Morgue was the project of Marco Corbelli, an Italian noise musician born in Sassuolo in 1970 who died in 2007. Working mostly with a Sequential Circuits Six-Trak synthesizer, Corbelli built his early catalogue on cassette through the industrial and noise “cassette culture” of the early 1990s, releasing on his own Slaughter Productions before moving to labels including Old Europa Cafe, Relapse and RRRecords through the late 1990s. Old Europa Cafe reissues three Atrax Morgue titles on 23 October. ‘Alive and Dead’ is a CD re-edition of a cassette the label sold out in 2018, remastered by Devi(L)s Granziera (Teatro Satanico) and adding two previously unreleased live recordings, from Treviso in 1999 and Tokyo in 2006. ‘Paranoia’, originally Atrax Morgue’s first full-length CD album, released on Old Europa Cafe in 2000, returns in an expanded edition remastered by Devis G., adding two alternate versions of the track “Il Forcipe di Thanatos” first issued on the 2017 “Malaplacenta” 7-inch; those alternate versions stem from a 2007 recording session, the year of Corbelli’s death. ‘Pathophysiology’, first released as a 1995 cassette and reprinted on CDr in 2002 and CD in 2019, is remastered again at Sweet Slaughter for this edition, with four previously unreleased bonus tracks, two recorded in 1995 and two in 2002. Nordvargr powers new Apex Parasite and Fistfun records Swedish musician Henrik Nordvargr Björkk, known as Nordvargr, recorded and contributed vocals to Swedish power electronics act Apex Parasite‘s new album ‘Warzone Europa’, tracked at Nar Mattaru over July and August 2026. The album is released as a hand-numbered edition of 199 copies. Björkk, also known for his work with Mz.412, Folkstorm and Bøltorn, also appears on ‘Not Nice Ever’, a harsh noise collaboration released as Fistfun with Claudio Frassine, known for his projects Mademoiselle Bistouri and North Central. ‘Not Nice Ever’ follows the pair’s earlier Fistfun release “Up the Rolls” and is limited to 199 hand-numbered copies. Black Leather Jesus and The Rita round out the batch American industrial power noise project Black Leather Jesus, founded by Richard Ramirez in 1989, releases ‘Probe’ in a limited edition of 300 copies. The album’s core lineup features Sean E. Ramirez, Nathan Golub, Thomas Puopolo, Richard Ramirez, Kevin Novak, JRL, Anjilla Ulfhednar, Scott Kindberg and Domokos, with individual tracks built around guest collaborations with slowdanger, G.X. Jupitter-Larsen, Yellow Gas Flames and The Rita. The Rita, the harsh noise project of Canadian musician Sam McKinlay, credited on Discogs with originating the “harsh noise wall” style and coining the term, also gets a reissue in the batch. ‘Possessed Nun Sleaze’ was first released in 1998 on Labyrinth Recordings, in an edition of 50 cassette copies, marking The Rita’s first release on an American label. Old Europa Cafe’s CD reprint carries new artwork and is dedicated to Isabella and Sister Angela.

items.body: Valencia label Industrial Complexx reissues the various-artists compilation “SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends” on double cassette and digital on October 15, 2026. The 18-track set, originally released by Unknown Pleasures Records in 2014, gathers international minimal synth, electro-punk and industrial acts covering the catalogue of Suicide’s Alan Vega and Martin Rev. SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends by Various Artists The reissue accompanies the Spanish-language publication of “Suicide, delincuentes electrónicos,” an essay on the band by musician and writer Pedro Peñas y Robles, originally published in French and English in 2024 and now released in Spanish by Industrial Complexx. The book traces the duo’s genesis and the chaotic sessions behind their 1977 debut album, drawing on testimony from scene figures including Marc Hurtado of Étant Donnés. ‘SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends’ contributors The tribute pairs Vega and Rev’s original catalogue with reinterpretations from Distel, Radical G, The Horrorist, David Carretta and Jürgen Engler of Die Krupps, Növö, Adan+Ilse featuring Gabi Delgado of D.A.F., Marc Hurtado performing with Alan Vega himself, Liebknecht featuring Kristoffer Grip of Agent Side Grinder, Unknown Celebrities, Laag, Position Parallele, Cruise [ctrl] featuring Richard 23 and Patrick Codenys of Front 242, The Present Moment, Absolute Body Control, Millimetric featuring Dirk Da Davo of The Neon Judgement, Black Egg featuring hausfrau, Simi Nah featuring KGB, and In Death It Ends featuring Usher of Norma Loy. Covered songs include “Che,” “Ghost Rider,” “Cheree,” “Frankie Teardrop,” “Dream Baby Dream” and “Diamonds, Fur Coat, Champagne.” Industrial Complexx describes the collection as channeling “the same abrasive, alienating and futuristic energy” that shaped Suicide’s catalogue. About Suicide Suicide was an American duo formed in New York City in 1970 by vocalist Alan Vega and instrumentalist Martin Rev, initially a trio with guitarist Paul Liebgott before continuing as a two-piece. The group paired Vega’s stream-of-conscious, rockabilly-inflected vocals with Rev’s minimal synthesizer and drum-machine backing, and was among the first acts to use the term “punk music” to describe itself, in 1970. Suicide independently released its debut album, “Suicide,” in 1977 on Red Star Records, featuring “Ghost Rider,” “Frankie Teardrop” and “Cheree.” A second album, “Suicide: Alan Vega and Martin Rev,” followed in 1980 on Ze Records, then “A Way of Life” in 1988, “Why Be Blue” in 1992 and the final studio album, “American Supreme,” in 2002. Vega and Rev also worked separately: Vega collaborated with Andrew Eldritch of The Sisters of Mercy as The Sisterhood in 1986, and with Alex Chilton and Ben Vaughn on “Cubist Blues” in 1996, while both released solo albums throughout their careers. Suicide played its final concert at London’s Barbican Centre on July 9, 2015, before Alan Vega died on July 16, 2016, at age 78. “SUICIDE Tribute To Iconic New York Legends,” first released via Unknown Pleasures Records in 2014, returns via Industrial Complexx on October 15, 2026, alongside the Spanish edition of Pedro Peñas y Robles’s book on the band.

items.body: Black Tape For A Blue Girl and Projekt Records reissue “The Rope” on October 2, presenting the 1986 debut album in a limited edition that pairs the original mix, remastered, with a new 2026 mix by Sam Rosenthal for its 40th anniversary. The 2LP edition is limited to 300 copies on 140-gram vinyl, with LP1 pressed on baby blue vinyl with black splatters and LP2 on transparent blue vinyl with white splatters. A 2CD digipak edition adds seven bonus tracks. Both formats are released via Projekt Records. “The Rope” is Black Tape For A Blue Girl’s debut album, the project Sam Rosenthal built around his songwriting and electronics, with Oscar Herrera on vocals. Each format includes the full 12-track album twice: the original 1986 mix, remastered, and the new 2026 mix. Martin Bowes of Attrition handled the mastering. The 2LP package adds a 16-page lyric and memorabilia fanzine insert plus a sticker; the 2CD edition comes in a 6-panel digipak with a 4-panel photo insert and sticker. The original 1986 tracklist runs: “memory, uncaring friend”, “hide in yourself”, “within these walls”, “the holy terrors”, “end”, “seven days til sunrise”, “the rope”, “the few remaining threads”, “the lingering flicker”, “slow blur”, “the floor was hard but home” and “we return”. The 2CD edition adds seven bonus tracks exclusive to that format: “the lingering flicker (first draft)”, “within these walls (early mix with clarinet)”, “the holy terrors (long)”, “second dream”, “the lingering flicker (isolated violins)”, “within these walls (short with violins)” and “memory, uncaring friend (remix intro)”. Sam Rosenthal on writing ‘The Rope’ Black Tape For A Blue Girl’s Rosenthal, who also founded Projekt Records, described the circumstances that produced the album: “In November ’85, following two years of recording instrumental electronic music, I invited Oscar Herrera to sing two songs on my ISLANDS cassette. A few months later in February of ’86 I left Florida for college in Orange, California. I was 20 years old, feeling isolated, lonely, missing friends back home. In my dorm room that spring I used the school’s Fostex 250 4-track cassette portastudio to record songs with my lyrics and melodies. Writing words for Oscar to sing over my ethereal and ambient music helped me explore those angsty and tangled feelings. The Rope is half vocal and half instrumental. It’s all quite minimal, yet it’s an album listeners still mention as a favorite. Capturing the confusion and darkness I felt at that time remains valid; new listeners connect with it today. I never would have expected that 40 years later The Rope would be listened to and appreciated by new generations. It’s really nice knowing those feelings are timeless, and the music has a place in people’s lives.” Uncut included “The Rope” in its “200 Greatest Goth Albums” feature, describing it as: “The vehicle for the more electronic songwriting of Projekt Records’ founder Sam Rosenthal, brought to life by singer Oscar Herrera’s arch delivery. BTFABG spun a unique thread of ambient darkwave, neoclassical exoticism and dark cabaret on their relatively bare-boned and lo-fi debut album.” The Rope (40th) by Black Tape For A Blue Girl About Black Tape For A Blue Girl Black Tape For A Blue Girl is the project Sam Rosenthal formed in 1986, built around his own songwriting and electronics and centered from the start on the pairing of his instrumental, ambient compositions with vocalists singing his lyrics. “The Rope”, released that year on Projekt Records, the label Rosenthal founded, introduced Oscar Herrera as vocalist alongside contributions from Allan Kraut, Kim Prior, Adam Buhler, Candy Sherlock and Lara Radford. The project’s discography continued through “Mesmerized by the Sirens” (1987), “Ashes in the Brittle Air” (1989), “A Chaos of Desire” (1991), “This Lush Garden Within” (1993), “Remnants of a Deeper Purity” (1996), “As One Aflame Laid Bare by Desire” (1999), “The Scavenger Bride” (2002), “Halo Star” (2004), “10 Neurotics” (2009), “Tenderotics” (2013), “These Fleeting Moments” (2016), “To Touch the Milky Way” (2018) and “The Cleft Serpent” (2021). Projekt has revisited several of these titles as anniversary reissues in recent years, including “The Cleft Serpent” and “Ashes in the Brittle Air” on vinyl, “Mesmerized by the Sirens” on vinyl and double CD, and “As One Aflame Laid Bare by Desire” and “Remnants of a Deeper Purity” in their own anniversary editions. Rosenthal has also continued to release music outside the project, including ambient and drone recordings under his own name. The 40th anniversary edition of “The Rope” extends that reissue campaign to the album that started it, presenting Herrera’s original vocal performances and Rosenthal’s 1986 arrangements alongside his 2026 revisiting of the same material.

items.body: Jah Wobble & The Invaders Of The Heart reissue the 2xCD collection “The Usual Suspects” on Dimple Discs on November 13, 2026. Originally released in 2017, the 23-track set has been unavailable for years and now changes hands at collectors’ prices; the digital edition is already available on Bandcamp, with the physical 2xCD prepared for that November date to coincide with a UK and Belgium tour. Usual Suspects by Jah Wobble & The Invaders Of The Heart “The Usual Suspects” gathers new recordings of Wobble’s solo material alongside songs from Invaders Of The Heart and his former band Public Image Ltd (PiL), drawn from a catalogue spanning almost forty years at the time of recording. The album was recorded at The Smokehouse studios in East London and opens with a version of PiL’s debut single “Public Image”, reworked from the band’s 1978 debut album. The tracklist also folds in cover versions of two film themes, “Midnight Cowboy” and “Get Carter”, plus Dawn Penn’s “You Don’t Love Me (No, No, No)” featuring vocalist Aurora Dawn, and a new take on “Visions Of You”, which originally featured Sinéad O’Connor on Invaders Of The Heart’s Mercury Prize-nominated 1992 album “Rising Above Bedlam”. The set closes with live recordings of “Liquidator” and “Poptones”, the latter drawn from PiL’s “Metal Box”. Recording personnel on “The Usual Suspects” comprised Jah Wobble on bass, vocals and percussion, Marc Layton-Bennett on drums, percussion and backing vocals, Martin Chung on guitars, George King on keyboards and backing vocals, Steve Rigby on programming and backing vocals, Sean Corby on trumpet and flugelhorn, Aurora Dawn on vocals, and Holly Macve on vocals. Of the band behind the album, Wobble said: “This band has been a delight to play with. Similar to my first early ’80s version of the Invaders, they can all really play, plus all genre bases […] are covered. It’s a big deal to me, because it’s like a 35 year old dream has finally been realised. This is how I heard The Invaders of the Heart sound all those years ago. A classy fusion of genres. Groovy, dubby but always changing and developing. Never standing still.” Tour dates for Jah Wobble & The Invaders Of The Heart The reissue follows a UK tour and comes ahead of Belgian dates in November. Confirmed shows: October 3 – Stourbridge, Katie Fitzgerald’s (UK) October 16 – Todmorden, Unitarian Church (UK) October 21 – Frome, The Tunnels (UK) October 22 – Bristol, The Fleece (UK) October 23 – Reading, Face Bar (UK) November 7 – London, Bush Hall (UK) November 25 – Hasselt, Club AFF (Belgium) November 26 – Bruges, Cactus Muziekcentrum (Belgium) November 27 – Oudenaarde, Harmonie Oudenaarde (Belgium) Tickets are available via Songkick. About Jah Wobble & The Invaders Of The Heart Jah Wobble, born John Wardle, is a bass guitarist and vocalist from East London who was the original bassist in Public Image Ltd alongside John Lydon from the band’s 1978 formation, co-writing and playing on the 1979 album “Metal Box” before leaving in late 1980. He formed Jah Wobble’s Invaders Of The Heart in 1982; that same period brought studio work alongside Can’s Holger Czukay and Jaki Liebezeit, U2 guitarist The Edge, and producer François Kevorkian. Invaders Of The Heart’s commercial peak came with 1991’s “Rising Above Bedlam”, nominated for the Mercury Prize, which included the UK top-40 single “Visions Of You” featuring Sinéad O’Connor. Wobble has since worked with artists including Ginger Baker, Björk, Brian Eno, Baaba Maal, Massive Attack, Sinéad O’Connor, Pharoah Sanders and his wife Zi Lan Liao on guzheng and harp. He reunited with former PiL guitarist Keith Levene in 2012 for the “Metal Box in Dub” shows and the album “Yin & Yang”. Jah Wobble & The Invaders Of The Heart recorded “The Usual Suspects” at The Smokehouse studios in East London, releasing it in 2017 following a six-month UK tour, as covered by Side-Line at the time. More recently, Wobble released the albums “Dub, Vol 1” (2025) and “Automated Paradise” (2026, with former Siouxsie & The Banshees guitarist Jon Klein) on Dimple Discs, and “Mystic Liverpool: The Beatles Psychedelic Songbook” with his sons, who record as Tian Qiyi, released by Cherry Red in August 2026. His autobiography, “Memoirs of a Geezer: Music, Life, Mayhem”, was published by Serpent’s Tail in 2009 and reissued in expanded form as “Dark Luminosity” by Faber & Faber in 2024. Dimple Discs now reissues “The Usual Suspects” as a 2xCD on November 13, 2026, timed to Jah Wobble & The Invaders Of The Heart’s UK and Belgium tour dates.

items.body: Room of Wires, the UK industrial/electronic duo of two producers who both go by Andrew, released the single “Skin weevil” on September 18, 2026, self-released on Bandcamp. The two-track release pairs the title track with “Do not leave a message” and arrives while the duo works on a new album. Skin weevil by Room of Wires Room of Wires bring an industrial and electronic sound that mixes hard-hitting rhythm programming with the duo’s usual dark ambient textures and field recordings. Both tracks on “Skin weevil” were written and produced by Room of Wires; the cover artwork is by the duo as well, with performance for camera by Fenia Kotsopoulou and photography by Daz Disley. Room of Wires’ ‘Skin weevil’ single The duo has not met in person: one member works with hardware and a tangle of physical wires, the other in software and virtual cables, sharing ideas and sounds over the internet. That process has produced “Skin weevil” as a standalone two-track single rather than part of a longer EP or album, released independently while the pair continue work on their next full-length. No further tracks or release date for that album have been announced. About Room of Wires Room of Wires is a UK industrial/electronic duo of two producers, both named Andrew, who write and record without ever having met, exchanging sounds and ideas remotely. Their debut EP, “Asylum sneaker”, appeared on Section27 in August 2014, followed by the Bandcamp-only “Dead skins” EP in November 2015, “Used as a runner” on Section27 in June 2016, “Black medicine” on Section27 in June 2017, and the remix-featuring “Mastakink” EP, self-released in October 2017. Their debut album, “White transit”, followed in November 2018, and the mini-LP “Test subject” arrived in October 2019. Room of Wires signed to the German label ant-zen for the albums “Plague of people” (April 2021) and “Welcome to the end game” (February 2023), releasing the “Fever switch” EP on Rednetic in October 2021 in between. Further self-released EPs followed with “Floodplains” (November 2023) and the album “If no other means are effective” in December 2025, the duo’s first full-length in close to three years. Alongside their own catalogue, Room of Wires record collaborative material as DasF and Cave like carving, and have contributed remixes and tracks to releases by Ah Cama-Sotz, Flint Glass, 4T Thieves and other acts. “Skin weevil” is their first new material since 2025’s “If no other means are effective”, released as the pair continue work on a new Room of Wires album.

items.body: Nine Inch Nails released their third studio album, “The Fragile,” through Nothing Records and Interscope Records on 21 September 1999. The industrial rock record arrived as a double album of 23 tracks running one hour and 43 minutes, split across two discs titled “Left” and “Right.” It turns 27 this year. Five years separated “The Fragile” from “The Downward Spiral.” Trent Reznor recorded and mixed the album at Nothing Studios in New Orleans between 1997 and 1999, producing it with Alan Moulder, who also engineered and mixed. Steve Albini handled supplemental drum recording at his Electrical Audio in Chicago, Tom Baker mastered at Precision Mastering, and Bob Ezrin was credited for final continuity and flow. Dr. Dre assisted with the mix on “Even Deeper.” Danny Lohner played guitars on six tracks and contributed drum programming and synthesizers, Adrian Belew added guitar to “Just Like You Imagined,” “The Great Below” and “Where Is Everybody?”, and Mike Garson played piano on “Just Like You Imagined,” “The Way Out Is Through” and “Ripe (With Decay).” Bill Rieflin drummed on “La Mer” alongside vocalist Denise Milfort, Jerome Dillon supplied chorus drums on “We’re in This Together,” and Charlie Clouser, Keith Hillebrandt and Steve Duda covered programming and sound design. David Carson took art direction, design and photography. Disc one, “Left,” runs “Somewhat Damaged,” “The Day the World Went Away,” “The Frail,” “The Wretched,” “We’re in This Together,” “The Fragile,” “Just Like You Imagined,” “Even Deeper,” “Pilgrimage,” “No, You Don’t,” “La Mer” and “The Great Below.” Disc two, “Right,” runs “The Way Out Is Through,” “Into the Void,” “Where Is Everybody?”, “The Mark Has Been Made,” “Please,” “Starfuckers, Inc.,” “Complication,” “I’m Looking Forward to Joining You, Finally,” “The Big Come Down,” “Underneath It All” and “Ripe (With Decay).” Three singles came from the album: “The Day the World Went Away” on 20 July 1999, “We’re in This Together” on 27 September 1999 and “Into the Void” on 10 January 2000, with “Starfuckers, Inc.” issued as a promotional single. The album entered the Billboard 200 at number one with first-week sales of 229,000 copies, the band’s first chart-topping album, then fell to number 16 the following week. The RIAA certified it double platinum on 4 January 2000, and it had sold 898,000 copies in the United States by May 2005. The US edition appeared as a two-CD tri-fold digipak; the three-LP vinyl pressing carried two tracks absent from the CD, “10 Miles High” and “The New Flesh,” and came in a gatefold sleeve with a 24-page booklet. In 2017 the album was reissued on vinyl as a Definitive Edition alongside “The Fragile: Deviations 1,” a limited four-LP instrumental set that was not pressed to CD. The album streams on Spotify. Sources differ on the exact day: MusicBrainz lists 20 September 1999, while Wikipedia, Discogs and Spotify all give 21 September 1999. About Nine Inch Nails Trent Reznor formed Nine Inch Nails in Cleveland, Ohio in 1988, writing and recording the project’s material during off-hours at Right Track Studio, where he worked as an engineer and janitor. TVT Records issued the debut album, “Pretty Hate Machine,” on 20 October 1989. The “Broken” EP followed in 1992, by which point Reznor had negotiated the Nothing Records imprint through Interscope, and “The Downward Spiral” arrived in 1994. Side-Line covered the 2019 book “Into The Never”, which examined that album’s cultural reach, and reported that Johnny Cash initially resisted recording “Hurt”, the “Downward Spiral” track he covered in 2002. “The Fragile” closed the 1990s for the band, and the remix album “Things Falling Apart” followed in 2000. Reznor returned with “With Teeth” in 2005, “Year Zero” in 2007, and both “Ghosts I-IV” and “The Slip” in 2008. Atticus Ross became a full member ahead of “Hesitation Marks” in 2013, and the pair have scored film and television alongside the band since. Side-Line has since reported on Reznor’s appearance on the deluxe vinyl reissue of the 1990 Pigface debut, the Future Ruins festival announced by Reznor and Ross in 2025, the “TRON Ares: Divergence” companion album, and the “Nine Inch Noize” collaboration with Boys Noize released in April 2026. “The Fragile” turns 27 this year, the record that took the band to number one in the United States for the first time.

items.body: Clan of Xymox, the Dutch darkwave and gothic rock project led by Ronny Moorings, released “Notes From The Underground” on 21 September 2001 through Pandaimonium Records in Europe. The album turns 25 this year. Metropolis Records issued it in North America nine days later, on 30 September 2001. Moorings wrote, recorded and mixed all twelve tracks, and produced the record with Mojca Zugna. It was the third studio album of the reformed Clan of Xymox era, after “Hidden Faces” from 1997 and “Creatures” from 1999. Three of its songs were already in circulation by the time it appeared. The “Liberty” CD single, issued by Pandaimonium on 20 October 2000 alongside the band’s double live album, carried “Liberty” together with “Number One” and “At Your Mercy”. Clan of Xymox’s ‘Notes From The Underground’ tracklist and credits The CD runs twelve tracks: “Innocent”, “I Want You Now”, “Internal Darkness”, “At Your Mercy”, “Anguish”, “Number One”, “Into Her Web”, “The Bitter Sweet”, “Liberty”, “Something Wrong”, “Mysterium” and “The Same Dream”. Dierk Budde mastered the album and Mojca Zugna made the sleeve artwork. The band’s official biography states the record reached number 2 on the German DAC chart and topped the US Musicfolio poll for 2001. The same page quotes a Side-Line review of the album as reading “This album is to be seen as a milestone in the band’s discography towards which their previous efforts all converge, or emerge from.” Pandaimonium returned to the material in May 2002 with “Remixes From The Underground”, a two-disc set that reworked every song on the album. Its contributors included Front 242, Assemblage 23, In Strict Confidence, Iris, Angels & Agony and Beborn Beton, and the limited edition added the band’s first video disc. Notes from the Underground by Clan Of Xymox About Clan of Xymox Ronny Moorings formed the band in 1981 in Nijmegen, the Netherlands. Its first release, the mini-album “Subsequent Pleasures”, appeared in 1983 in a run of 500 copies recorded on a four-track home setup. Demo material sent with it led to a deal with 4AD, and the self-titled album followed in 1985, cut at Palladium Studios in Edinburgh and co-produced with label head Ivo Watts-Russell. “Medusa” came next on the same label, and the band contributed “Muscoviet Musquito” to the 4AD compilation “Lonely Is An Eyesore” in 1987. The group parted with 4AD in October 1988, signed to Wing, a PolyGram subsidiary, and shortened its name to Xymox. “Twist of Shadows” arrived in 1989 with the singles “Obsession”, “Imagination” and “Blind Hearts”; the band’s official biography puts its sales above 300,000 copies. “Phoenix” followed in 1991 and closed the Wing chapter when PolyGram wound the label down. “Metamorphosis” and “Headclouds” then came out on the UK independent Zok Records. Moorings also wrote music for two CD-ROM games in the same period, “Total Mayhem” in 1996 and “Revenant” a year later. In 1997 Moorings ended the Xymox era, restarted the band as Clan of Xymox and signed to Tess Records. “Hidden Faces” appeared that year, produced by Dave M. Allen and John A. Rivers. “Creatures” followed in 1999, mixed by Rivers and Moorings, and moved the band to Metropolis Records in North America and Pandaimonium Records in Europe, the pairing that would also handle “Notes From The Underground”. The double live album “LIVE”, drawn from the band’s South and Central American shows, came out in October 2000. “Farewell” arrived in 2003, and “The Best Of Clan Of Xymox”, with its running order chosen by a fan poll, in September 2004. The “Weak In My Knees” EP opened 2006 ahead of the album “Breaking Point”. In early 2009 the band moved to Trisol Records in Europe while staying with Metropolis in the United States, and “In Love We Trust” came out on 18 August 2009, covered in Clan of Xymox’s ‘In Love We Trust’ turns 17 on 18 August. The thirteenth studio album “Darkest Hour” followed on 20 May 2011, the covers set “Kindred Spirits” in October 2012 and “Matters Of Mind, Body And Soul” on 14 February 2014. “Days Of Black” arrived on 7 April 2017, reported in Clan Of Xymox return with new album: ‘Days Of Black’. “Spider On The Wall” followed in 2020, announced in New Clan Of Xymox album ‘Spider On The Wall’ and video for ‘All I Ever Know’, and Moorings talked through his writing that September in Interview with Clan Of Xymox: ‘For Me A Lot Of These Memories Are Finished Stories Without A Soundtrack’. “Limbo”, written during the pandemic lockdowns, arrived in July 2021 and was previewed in Clan Of Xymox returns with all new album ‘Limbo’ in July. The eighteenth album “Exodus” followed in June 2024, reported in Clan Of Xymox announce new album for June: ‘Exodus’, with the “Blood of Christ” EP later that year and a 3CD edition of “Exodus” in February 2025. Moorings looked back across the full run in Ronny Moorings (Clan Of Xymox), an exclusive retrospective interview. Moorings has been the only constant member and still writes, records and produces the band’s music. The live line-up is Moorings on vocals, guitar and melodica, Mojca Zugna on bass, Mario Usai on guitar and bass, and Sean Winzer on keyboards, synth drums and backing vocals. Twenty-five years on, “Notes From The Underground” sits between “Creatures” and “Farewell” in that sequence.

items.body: Bristol project Allflaws released the album The Age Of Nefarious on September 21, 2026, through UK independent label Derelict State Records. The album runs 14 tracks over one hour and one minute, and is available to buy on iTunes and Amazon. Allflaws is the work of Gabriel Curran, who mixes industrial hip hop, trip hop, breakbeat, electronica and dark electronic music on “The Age Of Nefarious”. The album keeps heavy beats, distorted textures and atmospheric production under raw rap vocals, its atmosphere stays tied to Bristol trip hop, but the record leans harder into industrial hip hop’s heavier low end and lets experimental electronica break the production into fractured, glitching textures. Derelict State Records describes the album’s lyrics as exploring control, conformity, digital identity, cultures of violence, low-trust societies, and human resilience. Allflaws’ ‘The Age Of Nefarious’ pushes past the Bristol trip hop sound Derelict State Records, the independent UK label operating out of Bristol and London, works across trip hop, electronica, dub, breakbeat and the darker end of industrial music, including industrial hip hop, industrial electro and EBM. “The Age Of Nefarious” is distributed by Catapult, the same distributor behind Allflaws’ catalog since its earliest releases. An album trailer for “The Age Of Nefarious” is also online on YouTube. Side-Line previously covered Allflaws’ recent standalone singles, including “Vanity Matrix” in 2025, “Chimera” in 2024, and “Antifragile” in 2023. About Allflaws Allflaws was established in Bristol in 2004 by Gabriel Curran, who remains its only official member, writing, producing and performing every release. Curran’s vocal style combines rapping and singing with dark, poetic lyrics, and the project has built its sound around industrial, trip hop and breakbeat elements since its start. Allflaws signed to Catapult and Derelict State Records and released the album “These Walls Are Lies” in 2007, followed by the EPs “Ghost Of The System” and “Replicant Breed” and the album “Black Box Here After” in 2009. The singles “Escaping Sanity” (2010), “Amrak” (2011) and “Interfearence” (2011) preceded the “R Complex” EP and the single “Manufactured Violence” in 2012, and the album “Versus The Soul” in 2013. The album “Apparitions” followed in 2016, then “Mysterium” in 2019 and “Arcana” in 2021. Allflaws released the EP “Ghostrumentals” and the single “Becoming” in 2022, and the single “Antifragile” in 2024. “The Age Of Nefarious”, released September 21, 2026 on Derelict State Records, is Allflaws’ latest full-length, continuing the project’s industrial hip hop and trip hop direction two decades into Curran’s run with Allflaws.

items.body: This is Decca’s eighth release featuring Lise Davidsen, following hard on the heels of a Live at the Met recording released earlier this year. This is her first album devoted to Verdi, and it includes scenes from Macbeth, Un ballo in maschera, La forza del destino, Don Carlo and Aida. Verdi Amazon Presto Apple As readers surely know, Davidsen is considered by many to be one of today’s greatest operatic sopranos. The Metropolitan Opera’s Peter Gelb describes her as “the greatest Wagnerian talent since Birgit Nilsson and Kirsten Flagstad,” and conductor Antonio Pappano describes her voice as “one-in-a-million.” The singing on this album makes it hard to argue with such superlatives: Davidsen has tremendous power and consistency across an extended vocal range, although her control is such that she produces an impressively soft, silvery color when needed. The many high climactic notes heard in this recital ring out with a glistening brilliance that few can match. Yet despite this superb technique, not everything proved moving. I should acknowledge that I am not a fan of these “bleeding chunks” recitals. The publicity argues that there is a coherent framework for the selections, an exploration of the “emotional worlds of five remarkable women.” But with several selections lasting less than five minutes, a stop-and-start engagement is inevitable. The London Philharmonic plays wonderfully, with lots of energy, but sometimes there seems to be a generalized emotional mood from the podium that lessens the partnership between orchestra and singer. An impressive version of Nel dì della vittoria (track 1) opens the program. Davidsen captures the dark manipulative drive of Lady Macbeth, yet in Shirley Verrett’s two performances (La Scala/Abbado/DG and Teatro Comunale di Bologna/Chailly/Decca) I find an even more vivid characterization, even if Verrett’s is less opulent than Davidsen’s, and both Abbado and Chailly find more menace in the score. Lise Davidsen. Photo © Fredrik Arff. The three selections from Un ballo in maschera are more captivating (the orchestra also plays the Prelude to Act II, track 6). Both Ma dall’arido (track 8) and Morrò, ma prima in grazia (track 9) demonstrate Davidsen’s superb vocal control. In the latter she finds a heart-breaking vulnerability as she begs to see and hold her son before she dies (Kristina Blaumane’s cello solo adds to the potency of this aria). The accompaniment seems more engaged throughout these scenes. The selections from Don Carlo are excellent, though I find Callas’s willingness to act, even at the expense of vocal beauty, even more compelling. And I would be hard pressed to argue that Davidsen is more affecting or beautiful than Montserrat Caballé’s recording with the Covent Garden forces led by Carlo Maria Giulini (Warner Classics). The emotional temperature rises with the involvement of the Apollo Voices chorus in two selections from La forza del destino: La vergine degli angeli (track 11) is the most moving performance on the album. The recital closes with a wonderful reading of Ritorna vincitor! (track 15) from Aida, yet it does not eclipse Leontyne Price’s reading from her recording with forces from the Rome Opera House conducted by Solti (Decca). Despite the caveats mentioned above, this is an impressive achievement and there is no doubt that Davidsen’s many admirers will snap this up. It should also prove attractive to listeners who have yet to hear this uniquely gifted singer. Decca’s booklet is still unavailable on most digital media, which keeps many listeners from accessing full texts and context for recital programs like this one. items.body: One half of the Senior Staff was able to get out to a wholly non-ID:UD related gig over the weekend and catch Calgary’s Mares Of Thrace play a very rhythmically tight and cathartic set of doom metal. As we’ve briefly discussed here and there we’re both fans of a decent amount of metal covering a number of sub-genres, but neither of us are experts. Frankly, sometimes its nice to switch off the part of your brain that needs to be developing informed opinions and producing thoughtful analysis at all times and just enjoy some music simply because you dig it. But speaking of thoughtful analysis (?), let’s get you back to the home front with this week’s tracks. Dismantled Godflesh, “Master And Slave” Justin Broadrick announced earlier this year that he’d be winding Godflesh down for a second time some fifteen-odd years after its reactivation, but was planning two full LPs of new material before that time comes. The first such record sees release on Friday, and while the ratio of dub, electronic, and breaks elements which have always flitted about Godflesh releases had perhaps increased over the last few post-reunion albums, it’s hard not to think that Decay will be going right for the jugular Streetcleaner style based on its opening track. Turn it up and revel in the soothing annihilation of that bass tone. Decay by GODFLESH Grendel, “Dominion” It’s somehow been 7 years since the release of Grendel’s last LP Ascending the Abyss. It’s been a tangible absence in Our offices; JD Tucker has spent the last decade and a half redefining his legacy as an electro-industrial stylist and producer, starting with 2012’s genre-defying Timewave: Zero and the superlative Age of the Disposable Body, the latter being legitimately one of the most important political albums of the 2010s in Our Thing. “Dominion” speaks to the band we’ve come to know Grendel to be while showing some intriguing developments, such as JD’s now accomplished melodic vocal style, some very smooth string programming and sleek modern sound design applied to a classic EBM gallop. All that and lyrics that don’t just decry the social media era but examine the panopticon of control they emerge from? Welcome back Grendel, we missed you. Dominion by Grendel Dismantled, “Zero” Speaking of long-awaited returns, holy shit, there’s new Dismantled. Gary Zon’s long-running project has always been a standard bearer for a version of hard and harsh electro-industrial that maintains the genre’s atmospheric and emotional core. The first track from the forthcoming Endless is “Zero”, a cut that features Zon’s distinctive processed and multi-layered vocals, samples, and some fine string programming for good measure. It’s melancholic, but after a more than half a decade wait (the album was originally teased all the way back in 2021), it’s a sound that feels right. Endless by Dismantled Rosetta Stone, “Shadowban” Porl King’s moved Rosetta Stone through a number of preceding modes since reactivating the legendary second wave of goth rock project as a solo joint seven years back. A forthcoming release looks to keep that trend going (the Executing Nostalgia title feels rather on the nose in that regard) – one half of it will be made up of classic goth covers, continuing in the tradition of Unerotica and last year’s Nothing Is Sacred, while the other half is originals. This first taste of the latter feels like a callback to a very different moment in King’s history, though: the claustrophobic and hazy bass fog of this cut’s a dead ringer for the post witch house loops and grooves which made up the bulk of the voluminous In Death It Ends catalog in the 2010s. Shadowban by Rosetta Stone Control Fields, “Black Anomaly” Some solidly chewy bass sits at the centre of the B-side of the debut single from Tbilisi producer Control Fields, but that’s not the only thing which has us flashing back to 90s EBM and dark electro. The combo of icy programming and classic “hacking the Gibson” style sampling on this goes down as smooth as a Jolt cola being slammed during an all night Quake LAN party. Friction Code by Control Fields Emmon, “Relics (Kris Baha remix)” Kris Baha is one of the most reliable producers that emerged from the techno-body moment, with his canny grasp of gnarly sound design and how to assemble peak time bangers making him a go-to remixer for many artists. For evidece of why and the results why not check out Baha’s mix for Emmon’s “Relics”, taking the pensive and punchy original and giving it a slick peak-time makeover that references breakbeat driven 90’s techno, some psytrance, and some seriously warped synthwork. This’ll singe your nosehairs if you aren’t careful, play loud with caution. The post Tracks: September 21st, 2026 appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: Band: Kraanerg | Album: Aria for Labellum Tongues | Genre: Avant-prog | Year: 2026 From: Minneapolis, USA | Label: Independent For fans of: Frank Zappa, Papangu, Sigh, Cardiacs Bandcamp Kraanerg is the brainchild of composer and multi-instrumentalist Nat Bergrin, and Aria for Labellum Tongues is their third full-length release (and their second as a full band). This was my first exposure to Kraanerg, and I was very impressed by what I encountered. Western classical music plays a massive role on this record, both in terms of instrumentation and structure. Plenty of bands will shoehorn in some violin, but not many display the ability to integrate classical influences quite like this band does. “Amargosa Raga” kicks the album off with strange, discordant guitar lines. The vocal line is surprisingly melodic for the harsh, microtonal backing, and there’s some great supporting saxophone. Classical elements play a significant role here as well, with violin and piano taking the lead on various passages. What began as a fairly harsh piece gradually evolves into a lush composition, evoking many of the Mellotron-heavy greats of the classic prog era, but run through a more modern and uncompromisingly weird lens. The title track comes next, with an onslaught of buzzy guitars, swooping strings, and tinkling vibraphone. The classical influences on this track tread a fine line between sweet and creepy, with the violin frequently adding a remorseful edge.  “Blessings in Silk, Saffron, and Naran-Ji” nearly feels like a new wave song in its opening moments. There’s a bright hopefulness, but that soon gives way to a stripped-back classical passage. Piano, violin, and scratchy clean guitar float about. The intensity of the song gradually swells with the addition of drums and wordless vocals, lifting everything upward, but with an underlying sense of tension. When rock elements eventually take the lead again, violin remains the most prominent instrument. There’s an irrepressible sense of drama, and the somewhat rough vocals feel genuinely emotional. This piece is followed by the only song under four minutes on the album, “Anguloa Virginalis (Um Rosto de Mulher)”. It’s a light and airy breather following the intensity of the previous song. Piano, vibraphone, and delicate percussion evoke loungey jazz. Gothic organ and distorted guitar kicks off “Iron Sign of the Masdevallia”. Syncopated drums and piano give this track a disorienting feel, and the dense arrangement is smothering. As the song enters an instrumental section, sax and piano both get ample time in the spotlight, each one painting a dramatic picture. Next, the song takes a surprisingly sunny turn, with piano plinking out over a (mostly) major-key backing. The guitars borrow a lot from punk, but just about everything else is more clearly indebted to classical music, which makes for an interesting contrast. This artsy punk-fusion continues as this epic enters its final few minutes. The chords become more chaotic and irregular, and the vocals become more unhinged. The music is intense, yet oddly joyous, like Cardiacs’ best work. The opening gothic passage comes back for a closing reprise, which ties things up beautifully. The album ends on its longest song, the 20-minute “Visible to the Wrong Faces”. In comparison to the storming tempo of the previous song, this one is quite restrained in its opening. Classical music predominates for the first few minutes, led by piano and saxophone. It isn’t until about four minutes in that any rock elements enter, when buzzing guitars and stomping drums begin to play supporting roles. When vocals finally enter, the music is noisy with a sense of carefully-crafted chaos. Vibraphone and violin support jangly, post-punk guitars, and the vocal melody draws from avant-garde music. Throughout this whole album, the band has shown that they are masters of textural variation and contrast, and the second half of this song is a prime example. Post-metal, classical music, and classic prog influences are all evident, and everything gels into a satisfying conclusion. Aria for Labellum Tongues is a highly ambitious and very successful musical statement. The blending of rock and classical structures is pulled off wonderfully, and each of the songs on this album feels thoughtfully put-together. It’s a long and challenging record, but it’s well worth your time. Score: 95/100
